## TL;DR

The review ceiling is now configurable as `review.timeoutMinutes` (default 15, clamped 1–240), exposed as a live Settings number field with a `getConfigSchema()` entry, a supported TOML key, and documentation. A pass stopped by the ceiling is recorded as a timeout — not as "no usable report" — in the task activity line and the Review tab, and RepoOS schedules exactly one automatic retry before falling back to a human. Timeout classification, persistence, and the single-retry bound are covered by a new test file.

## Work and rationale

`src/server/review.ts` previously armed every review with a private `REVIEW_TIMEOUT_MS = 900_000`. I replaced it with `reviewTimeoutMinutes(config)` / `reviewTimeoutMs(config)` helpers, stored the armed value on the `Run` record, and used it for both freshly spawned and reload-adopted reviews. This matters across a server reload: the finishing process reports the timeout that actually stopped the pass rather than whatever the current config happens to say.

I kept the existing report `state` values (`ok` / `incomplete` / `failed`) and added a structured `timedOut` flag plus `timeoutMinutes`. That is backward compatible with every existing report and UI consumer, while letting the drawer label the failure "Review timed out" and render an amber timeout card instead of a red crash card. The flag and minutes persist in the cached and tracked pass frontmatter (`timed_out`, `timeout_minutes`), so the Review tab can explain the stop after a reload or on a fresh clone.

The activity summary in `src/core/review-passes.ts` now takes an optional timeout detail. A timeout reads `review pass N: timed out after 15 minutes — no report (retrying once automatically)` on the first pass and `… — no report; human needed` after the retry, leaving the old "failed — no usable report" wording for genuine silent exits. That directly removes the misleading #1013 message.

The retry is bounded by `review_timeout_retries` in task frontmatter and an in-process map that closes the window before the live index observes the file write. Scheduling persists the counter first, then waits four seconds before starting a `timeout-retry` pass. A successful or incomplete pass clears the counter for a future episode. The first timeout intentionally does not set `needsInput`; only an exhausted retry does, so a slow model gets its second chance without paging a human. The retry appears in the activity note and in the task log marker.

I considered automatic scaling by changed-file count, which the task allowed, but chose an explicit timeout plus a bounded retry. A file-count multiplier is hard to explain when it still guesses wrong for a slow model, and it would need a git diff before arming every timeout. The setting is discoverable in Settings and documented in `user-docs/configuration.md` with the 1–240 clamp and the retry behaviour.

## Approaches tried

My first report shape used a new `state: "timed-out"`, but that would touch every server and UI branch that switches on report state. A boolean flag on the existing `failed` state kept the change narrow. I also checked whether the retry marker would survive `run()`'s session reset; it does not, so the durable activity note is the canonical record and the log line carries the rest.

## Challenges and blockers

The first scoped check failed on a TypeScript mock tuple in my new test, then on an older `review-override` assertion that pinned `finalizeRun` to six arguments. I added the new `timeoutMinutes` argument to that expectation and reran. Remote validation retried once after a host hang and then failed on the real test assertion, not on infrastructure.

## Key learnings

- Persist a retry counter before scheduling it; in-memory state alone does not survive a reload, and the file write alone does not close the race before the index catches up.
- Distinguish "the agent was stopped" from "the agent exited silently" at the point of failure. Both produce no report, but only one deserves an automatic retry.
- `repoos check --changed main` reuses remote validation, so a test-only type error still costs a full remote round trip; run a local build first.
